paragraphs.text: The Rav opens by showing that Parshas Toldos is full of blessing: every aliyah contains a bracha, and he counted thirty-two words from the root of bracha in it. Toldos is the sixth sedra, and six is a number of blessing. The Jews in Mitzrayim were blessed with six children at a time, and Yosef, the sixth of the ushpizin, had his blessing doubled into two shevatim.

The root of bracha itself spells doubling: beis is two, chaf twenty and reish two hundred. This is why, he says, chassidim treat shishi as the most important aliyah and put the most joy into the sixth hakafah. Yet to receive blessing a person must be whole, like a pocket without a hole, since the Mishnah teaches that only shalom is a vessel that holds blessing; so the Rav says one should pray for shalom among Jews.

Putting the subject of emunah aside for the sedros of Yetzias Mitzrayim and Matan Torah, the Rav turns to the passuk contrasting Esav the hunter with Yaakov who sat and learned, and Yitzchak loved Esav for his hunting. Rashi explains that Esav trapped his father as a hunter traps an animal; Onkelos, that Yitzchak ate from his hunting.

Both are hard. The Rav cannot accept that Yitzchak would prefer Esav for a steak, nor that such a tzaddik could be fooled. The same pattern returns at the brachos, which Yitzchak makes depend on Esav's dish.

blocks.heading: The day the bechorah was sold

paragraphs.text: Going back to the start of the sedra, the Rav brings Rashi that the bechorah was sold on the day Avraham Avinu passed away. A mourner's first meal comes from others and should be round, so Yaakov cooked lentils for Yitzchak, just as the round egg on the Seder plate recalls mourning for the Beis Hamikdash.

That day Esav came home starving after five sins. He killed Nimrod to take the garment Hashem made for Adam, which drew animals to the hunter, and he denied techiyas hameisim, one of the thirteen principles of faith. This made him an apikores, whose shechitah may not be eaten, and the Rav asks how Yitzchak could eat his meat all those years.

The passuk says 'the boys grew up', and Rashi explains that at thirteen their natures became evident. But Yitzchak was sixty at their birth and Avraham died at a hundred seventy-five, so that day they were fifteen. Some say Rashi is misprinted; the Rav asks why, then, the passuk would call them grown only at fifteen.

blocks.heading: All one's days come on the last day

paragraphs.text: The Rav asks how Eliyahu could grant Elisha double his own spirit, as Melachim tells, and why only if Elisha saw him taken up. One cannot give what one does not have, yet Elisha did perform double Eliyahu's wonders.

He answers with the Agra deKallah and the Bnei Yissaschar that time is a creation. As the Zohar says, each day comes down, is inscribed with a person's deeds and ascends, so teshuvah is easier before it goes up. On a person's last day all his days return to escort him; so Moshe said that today he had his hundred twenty years, and only then is he called 'the man of G-d'.
Eliyahu on his last day was therefore far greater and could give double. The Chasam Sofer, in a hesped in his derashos, grieved that he was not at his rebbe Rabbi Nosson Adler's bedside.

blocks.heading: Every tzaddik has his opposing rasha

paragraphs.text: The Gemara in Chagigah tells that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya, who always won debates on faith with the non-Jews, comforted his students on his deathbed: when he is gone, his opponents will lose their strength too. From this the Rav explains that every tzaddik has a rasha of his own measure who keeps the scale balanced, so that the choice between good and bad stays even.
Avraham's opponent was Nimrod, whose name comes from rebellion: Avraham spread belief in one G-d, Nimrod rebellion against Him. Therefore Nimrod was killed the very day Avraham passed away.

blocks.heading: Kedushah at one bedside, tumah at the other

paragraphs.text: Likewise Esav was Yaakov's lifelong opponent, and the Gemara in Sotah relates that he died on the day of Yaakov's burial: he claimed a share in the Me'aras HaMachpelah, and while Naftali ran to Mitzrayim for the deed, Chushim ben Dan cut off his head.

Returning to the day of Avraham's passing, the Rav explains that Yaakov stood at his bedside, where all of Avraham's hundred seventy-five years came down, and like Elisha he absorbed great kedushah. Esav stood by the slain Nimrod amid the tumah of all his sins and absorbed it. So both 'grew up' that day at fifteen, one a great tzaddik, the other a great rasha.

Therefore Yaakov said 'sell me as this day': what this day made of them decides who needs the bechorah. The tzaddik lives by 'today to do them, tomorrow their reward'; the rasha, as the navi puts it, says 'eat and drink, for tomorrow we die'. Esav agreed that by his view he had no need of it.

blocks.heading: A tzaddik tastes kedushah, not flavor

paragraphs.text: Years later Yitzchak sends Esav for good food. The Rav explains that a real tzaddik enjoys life, feeling the sweetness of Torah and mitzvos, but measures food only by its kedushah. The Yismach Moshe once warmed the wrong pot and ate soapy water for supper without noticing.

Kedushah enters food through intention: a wife who cooks carefully kosher food so her family can serve Hashem, especially for Shabbos, puts kedushah into it. Matzah, prepared 'for the sake of the mitzvah' from the harvest on, is the holiest food, and the korban Pesach became holy through words.
From the day Esav became an apikores, the Rav says, Yaakov prepared Yitzchak's food and let Esav bring it, since Yitzchak would sense treif; the Gemara says even tzaddikim's animals refuse it.

blocks.heading: The Slonimer Rebbe and the borrowed plates

paragraphs.text: The Rav tells a story he heard from an eyewitness. The Slonimer Rebbe, visiting Yerushalayim, dined with a poor, beardless, G-d-fearing man, but did not touch the fish and asked for a big plate. The plates were borrowed from a man with a long beard, who admitted he had not immersed them, relying on poskim. The Rebbe told the host that above they would ask him 'where is your beard?', and the other 'where is your Jew?'

blocks.heading: Yitzchak's mistake and the day of the brachos

paragraphs.text: Tasting kedushah in food brought by a hunter who did not learn, Yitzchak concluded that Esav was a concealed tzaddik, one of the thirty-six, greater than a revealed one. On Pesach night Rivka's prophecy, as the Targum says, forced Yaakov to bring the food himself, and Rashi says Yitzchak sensed Gan Eden. Esav found nothing and brought a dog, says Targum Yonasan, and Yitzchak sensed Gehinnom. So Onkelos and Rashi agree.
He closes with a tzaddik whose chulent no recipe could copy, because each Friday he threw in a handful of beans himself; that, the Rav says, is what tzaddikim taste.
